name: Brain Computer Interfaces
title: Brain Computer Interfaces
answer: Brain computer interfaces are systems that read neural signals and translate them into commands for external devices, or write signals into the brain. In medical AI, the scope includes motor neuroprosthetics, communication for people with locked-in syndrome, sensory restoration, and closed-loop neuromodulation. The field spans invasive implants, partially invasive electrocorticography, and non-invasive EEG or fNIRS. This site covers brain computer interfaces as part of neuroinformatics and the brain, alongside other medical AI models.

sections.body: Brain computer interfaces are systems that read neural signals and translate them into commands for external devices, or write signals into the brain. In medical AI, the scope includes motor neuroprosthetics, communication for people with locked-in syndrome, sensory restoration, and closed-loop neuromodulation. The field spans invasive implants, partially invasive electrocorticography, and non-invasive EEG or fNIRS. This site covers brain computer interfaces as part of neuroinformatics and the brain, alongside other medical AI models.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Brain computer interface systems run on implanted electrode arrays, electrocorticography grids, or scalp EEG caps, connected to amplifiers and signal processors. The decoding software often runs on bedside computers, embedded processors in the implant, or cloud services for offline analysis. Latency and power constraints are tight for implanted devices, so many use dedicated neural processing units or low-power microcontrollers. Data pipelines include real-time filtering, spike sorting, and feature extraction before a model maps features to control outputs.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with recording neural activity, then cleaning and aligning signals to behavioral or intended outputs. Common methods include Kalman filters for continuous movement decoding, linear discriminant analysis for discrete selections, and deep learning models such as recurrent networks for sequence prediction. Training often uses supervised sessions where the user imagines or attempts a movement while the system records paired neural and kinematic data. Calibration is repeated because neural signals drift over days and weeks.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Brain computer interface data is intimate and can reveal mood, intent, or cognitive state, so consent, data minimization, and secure storage are central. Implanted devices carry surgical risk, infection risk, and long-term hardware failure, while non-invasive systems raise fewer physical risks but lower signal quality. Product liability questions are active, and this site tracks six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, some of which involve medical devices. Provenance matters for training data because datasets are small, often from a single patient, and may not transfer across individuals.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward fully implanted wireless systems with higher channel counts and longer battery life. Researchers are working on bidirectional interfaces that both read and write to the brain for sensory feedback and closed-loop therapy. Regulatory pathways are still forming for adaptive algorithms that change over time, and the site's 210 compliance and regulation pages reflect that uncertainty. Over the next decade, brain computer interfaces may expand from assistive technology for severe disability into broader rehabilitation and cognitive monitoring, but clinical evidence will need to catch up with engineering progress.
